items.title: Female Reproductive Cycle - The Menstrual Cycle

source_refs.note: Topic 17.1.3 with the For Information boxes on menopause and hCG (PDF 79-82); Figures 17.6 and 17.7 are replaced by the original diagram. The chapter's exercises (PDF 81-82) are not part of the lesson body.

blocks.text: The female reproductive system works through a series of cyclic events, the menstrual cycle, which lasts about a month (28 days on average) and has three phases.

items: Menstrual phase (days 1 to 5): the functional layer of the endometrium is shed, and the tissue and blood leave the body (menstruation) for 3 to 5 days, because estrogen and progesterone are low. FSH begins to rise.

Proliferative phase and ovulation (days 6 to 14): the rise in FSH makes a few follicles grow, but only one, the Graafian follicle, matures and rises to the ovary's surface while the others degenerate. FSH makes it secrete estrogen, which rebuilds the endometrium, making it velvety, thick and supplied with blood. At the end of this phase (day 14) a sudden release of LH from the anterior pituitary makes the Graafian follicle release the ovum into the oviduct: ovulation.

Secretory (post-ovulatory) phase (days 15 to 28): LH turns the ruptured follicle into a yellow corpus luteum, which secretes estrogen and progesterone that make the endometrium more vascular and glandular. If fertilization does not occur, the corpus luteum degenerates, LH secretion stops, estrogen and progesterone fall abruptly and the thickened endometrium is shed with bleeding: menstruation on day 28.

blocks.alt: Section of an ovary with blood vessels entering at the left. Stages are arranged clockwise, with arrows outside: primary follicles with primary oocytes, developing follicles growing a fluid space, a large Graafian follicle with its secondary oocyte, a ruptured follicle with the released ovum leaving the ovary, then early corpus luteum, corpus luteum and corpus luteum regressed.
blocks.caption: Figure 17.6: Changes in ovary during menstrual cycle (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 17.6).

blocks.alt: Chart of days 0 to 28 in three rows, divided into the menstrual phase, follicular phase, ovulation at day 14 and secretory phase. Ovary: a follicle grows, ruptures at ovulation, becomes a corpus luteum and regresses. Hormone levels: FSH rises early with a small peak at ovulation; estrogen peaks just before ovulation and again around day 21; LH surges at day 13 to 14; progesterone peaks around day 22. Endometrium: shed in the first days, then thickens until late in the cycle.
blocks.caption: Figure 17.7: Menstrual cycle (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 17.7; phase label spelled 'Secretory', menstrual phase line at day 5).

blocks.title: Pregnancy and menopause
blocks.text: If the egg is fertilized, the tiny embryo secretes human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG), which keeps the corpus luteum alive, so estrogen and progesterone stay high and menstruation is prevented; because hCG comes from the embryo's chorion and not the mother, it is the hormone that pregnancy tests detect. The cycles stop at around 50 years of age: menopause.
